name: LBC Optimize Images
author: Rinku Y

sections.description:
LBC Optimize Images is a highly efficient, lightweight WordPress plugin designed to automatically optimize your images by converting them to next-generation formats: AVIF and WebP.

Instead of replacing or permanently altering your original images, this plugin creates optimized copies and seamlessly serves them to your visitors. This drastically reduces page load times and improves your Google PageSpeed Insights and Core Web Vitals scores without any risk to your original media.

Features

  • Next-Gen Formats: Automatically converts JPEG and PNG images to AVIF (primary) and WebP (fallback).
  • Dual Delivery System: Uses both .htaccess rewrite rules and HTML Output Buffering to guarantee the images are served across all server types.
  • 100% Server Compatibility: Works flawlessly on Apache, LiteSpeed, Nginx, and IIS, as well as localhost environments (like WAMP/XAMPP).
  • Zero Risk to Originals: Your original images are completely untouched. Optimized copies are safely stored in a separate wp-content/uploads-lbcimg/ directory.
  • Bulk Optimization: A built-in 1-click bulk optimizer allows you to process all your existing media library images seamlessly in the background.
  • Customizable Quality: Easily adjust the compression quality for both AVIF and WebP formats directly from the settings page.
  • Block Theme Compatible: Works perfectly with classic themes and modern Full Site Editing (FSE) block themes.
  • Clean Uninstall: If you ever uninstall the plugin, it completely cleans up after itself by deleting all optimized images and removing its configuration options.

How it Works

  1. When you upload a new image (or run the Bulk Optimizer), the plugin creates optimized .avif and .webp copies of the image using your server’s native Imagick or GD libraries.
  2. These copies are stored in a dedicated folder (uploads-lbcimg/uploads/) mirroring your media library structure.
  3. When a visitor loads a page, the plugin intercepts the HTML before it is sent to the browser and automatically changes the image URLs to point to the new .avif or .webp files.
  4. For servers running Apache or LiteSpeed, it also generates .htaccess rewrite rules as a secondary fallback.

Backup Methods

Since LBC Optimize Images never alters or deletes your original uploaded images, no special backup methods are required! Your original files remain exactly where they are in the wp-content/uploads/ directory. If you ever deactivate the plugin, WordPress will immediately revert to serving your original images.
sections.installation:
1. Upload the lbc-optimize-images folder to the /wp-content/plugins/ directory.
  2. Activate the plugin through the ‘Plugins’ menu in WordPress.
  3. Navigate to the new LBC Optimize Images menu in your WordPress dashboard.
  4. (Optional) Adjust the WebP and AVIF quality settings to your preference.
  5. Click Optimize Existing Images to run the bulk optimizer for your past uploads.
sections.faq:
Does this delete my original images?

No! Your original images are never touched. The plugin creates optimized copies in a completely separate directory (wp-content/uploads-lbcimg/).

What happens if I uninstall the plugin?

Upon uninstallation, the plugin will automatically delete the uploads-lbcimg folder (removing all optimized copies to free up disk space) and clean up its database settings. Your website will instantly revert back to using your original images.

Will it work on Nginx or IIS?

Yes! By default, the plugin uses an HTML rewriting engine which works on all servers, including Nginx and IIS. Ensure the “Serve Optimized Images” toggle is set to ON in the plugin settings.

Can I use this on localhost?

Yes! Because the plugin uses intelligent URL path extraction and HTML rewriting, it works perfectly on local environments like WAMP, XAMPP, and LocalWP.

What if my server doesn’t support Imagick?

The plugin uses a smart fallback system. It first attempts to use the Imagick PHP extension (which provides the best quality and AVIF support). If Imagick is not installed, it gracefully falls back to using the native PHP GD library to handle WebP conversions.
